name: Tsaang Gubat
shortDescription: An evergreen shrub native to the Philippines and other parts of Asia. Its leaves have been scientifically validated for anti-diarrheal, analgesic, and antimicrobial properties. It is one of the 10 medicinal plants endorsed by the Philippine Department of Health and has been formulated into a Philippine FDA-approved tablet for biliary and gastrointestinal colic.

preparation.description: Boil 5–6 fresh leaves in 2 cups of water for 10 minutes. Strain and drink while warm.
Crush fresh leaves into a paste and apply directly to the affected area.
Tsaang gubat tablet has been formulated and registered with the Philippine Food and Drug Administration (FDA) after Phase I–III clinical trials. Listed in the Philippine National Formulary.

facts.habitat: Tropical lowland forests; grows wild in disturbed areas and open fields

warnings: Consult a doctor before using for medicinal purposes.
Do not consume in excessive amounts.
Avoid use if allergic to plants in the Boraginaceae family.
Pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before use.
Not a substitute for professional medical treatment.

cultivationGuide.soil: Well-drained, loamy to sandy soil; tolerates poor soil
cultivationGuide.sunlight: Full sun to partial shade (4–6 hours daily)
cultivationGuide.growthTime: 1–2 years to reach usable size; shrub matures at 1.5–4 meters
tips: Prune regularly to encourage bushy growth.
Harvest leaves before flowering for highest potency.
Can be grown as a hedge or ornamental shrub.

research.title: Evaluation of the bioactivity of triterpene mixture isolated from Carmona retusa (Vahl.) Masam leaves
research.summary: The major constituent of C. retusa leaves is a triterpene mixture (α-amyrin, β-amyrin, and bauerenol). At 100 mg/kg, the triterpene mixture exhibited 51% analgesic activity and 29% anti-diarrheal activity (charcoal tracing test), which increased to 55% at 250 mg/kg. The triterpene mixture showed moderate antimicrobial activity against S. aureus, C. albicans, and T. mentagrophytes. Results were comparable to mefenamic acid (a commercial NSAID) at α = 0.01.
research.reference: Villaseñor IM, Canlas AP, Faustino KM, Plana KG. J Ethnopharmacol. 2004 May;92(1):53–6. DOI: 10.1016/j.jep.2004.01.017

research.title: Ehretia microphylla Tablet Formulation for Biliary and Gastrointestinal Colic: A Review of its Phytochemical Constituents, Pharmacologic Activities and Clinical Researches
research.summary: Comprehensive review of tsaang gubat's phytochemical constituents (flavonoids, phenolics, triterpenes, alkaloids) and pharmacologic activities (antibacterial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-diarrheal, anti-angiogenesis, wound healing, anti-cancer). The tsaang gubat tablet has been granted a full patent and is registered with the Philippine FDA. It is listed in the Philippine National Formulary after Phase I–III clinical trials.
research.reference: Legaspi CLB, Bagaoisan DM. Acta Medica Philippina. 2020 Feb;54(1):80–85. DOI: 10.47895/amp.v54i1.1108

research.title: Ehretia genus: a comprehensive review of its botany, ethnomedicinal uses, phytochemistry, and pharmacology
research.summary: Comprehensive review of the Ehretia genus covering botany, ethnomedicinal uses, phytochemistry, and pharmacology. Confirms anti-diarrheal, anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antibacterial, and antioxidant properties of E. microphylla. Identifies key bioactive compounds including triterpenes and rosmarinic acid.
research.reference: Jiang S et al. Frontiers in Pharmacology. 2025. DOI: 10.3389/fphar.2025.1526359

comparisonTraits.leaf: Small, rounded, obovate leaves approximately 1–2.5 cm in length with lobed apex and short bristly hairs
comparisonTraits.flower: Small white flowers, axillary, solitary or in pairs on a slender hairy peduncle
comparisonTraits.stem: Highly branched, divaricate with brown bark approximately 3 mm thick
comparisonTraits.smell: Mild, herbal tea-like scent when leaves are crushed

name: Tawa-tawa
shortDescription: An annual herb widely distributed in tropical regions including the Philippines. Known for its traditional use in managing dengue fever and thrombocytopenia. Clinical studies have shown it can help increase platelet counts. It also has antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antimalarial properties.

preparation.description: Boil 1 cup of fresh whole plant (roots, stems, leaves) in 2 cups of water for 15 minutes. Strain and drink warm, 1 cup 3 times daily.
Crush fresh leaves and apply as a paste to cuts, wounds, and skin irritations.
Steep dried aerial parts in hot water for 10 minutes. Strain and drink.

facts.origin: Tropical Americas; naturalized worldwide in tropical regions
facts.habitat: Waste places, roadsides, lawns, and disturbed areas in tropical regions

warnings: Consult a doctor before using for medicinal purposes, especially for dengue.
Do not consume in excessive amounts; the plant contains latex which can be irritating.
Avoid contact with latex sap — it may cause skin and eye irritation.
Not a substitute for professional medical treatment for dengue fever.
Pregnant women should avoid use due to potential uterine stimulant effects.
Euphorbia hirta should not be the sole treatment for severe thrombocytopenia.

cultivationGuide.soil: Adaptable; grows in sandy, loamy, and clay soils; tolerates poor soil
tips: Grows readily as a weed; collect from open fields or grow in a garden pot.
Harvest the whole plant when flowering for maximum potency.
No special fertilization needed.

research.title: Management of thrombocytopenia and flu-like symptoms in dengue patients with herbal water of Euphorbia hirta
research.summary: A clinical study of 125 dengue patients showed that over 70% of patients had improvement in platelet count, white blood cell count, fever, and flu-like symptoms after consuming herbal water of E. hirta. Leucopoenia improved significantly after use of the aqueous extract.
research.reference: Mir M, Khurshid R, Aftab R. J Ayub Med Coll Abbottabad. 2012 Jul-Dec;24(3-4):6–9. PMID: 24669596

research.title: Potential Use of Euphorbia hirta for Dengue: A Systematic Review of Scientific Evidence
research.summary: Systematic review confirming that E. hirta has significantly increased platelet counts in both animal models and clinical studies of dengue patients. Mean platelet count was increased by 80% following E. hirta treatment for 9 days in one clinical study. The plant shows promise as a complementary treatment for dengue.
research.reference: Perera SD, Kumarasinghe G, Abeysinghe M. Evid Based Complement Alternat Med. 2018. DOI: 10.1155/2018/2048530

research.title: Euphorbia hirta: Its chemistry, traditional and medicinal uses, and pharmacological activities
research.summary: Comprehensive review (cited 479 times) covering the chemistry, traditional uses, and pharmacological activities of E. hirta. Confirmed antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiarrheal, anti-asthmatic, and antiviral properties. Key phytochemicals include quercetin, gallic acid, tannins, and flavonoids.
research.reference: Kumar S, Malhotra R, Kumar D. Pharmacogn Rev. 2010;4(8):174–184. DOI: 10.4103/0973-7847.70915

comparisonTraits.leaf: Small, hairy, oblong leaves with a reddish-purple center spot, arranged oppositely on hairy stems
comparisonTraits.flower: Tiny reddish flowers clustered in the leaf axils
comparisonTraits.stem: Hairy, prostrate or erect stems that exude milky latex when broken
comparisonTraits.smell: Mild, slightly pungent herbal scent

name: Oregano (Cuban Oregano)
shortDescription: A succulent perennial herb with aromatic leaves, widely used in traditional medicine. Scientifically confirmed to have strong antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and wound healing properties. The essential oil contains carvacrol and thymol, which are potent antimicrobial compounds.

preparation.description: Boil 5–6 fresh leaves in 1 cup of water for 5–10 minutes. Strain and drink warm. For children, add honey.
Crush fresh leaves and extract juice. Mix with honey for a soothing cough syrup. Take 1 teaspoon 2–3 times daily.
Crush fresh leaves into a paste and apply to the affected area for insect bites, rashes, or minor wounds.

facts.origin: Native to Southern and Eastern Africa; naturalized throughout the tropics
facts.habitat: Tropical and subtropical gardens; thrives in warm, dry conditions

warnings: Consult a doctor before using for medicinal purposes.
Do not consume essential oil directly — it is highly concentrated.
May cause allergic reactions in some individuals.
Pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before use.
Avoid prolonged use of essential oil on skin without dilution.

cultivationGuide.soil: Well-drained, sandy to loamy soil; tolerates drought
cultivationGuide.sunlight: Full sun to partial shade (6 hours daily)
cultivationGuide.watering: Water moderately; allow soil to dry between waterings (succulent plant)
cultivationGuide.growthTime: Rapid growth; harvestable in 4–6 weeks from cuttings
tips: Very easy to grow from stem cuttings in pots or garden beds.
Prune regularly to encourage bushy growth.
Can be grown indoors near a sunny window.
Drought-tolerant — avoid overwatering.

research.title: Plectranthus amboinicus (Lour.) Spreng: A multi therapeutic agent — A review
research.summary: Comprehensive review (cited 519 times) confirming numerous pharmacological properties including antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antitumor, wound healing, anti-epileptic, larvicidal, and antidiabetic activities. The essential oil is rich in carvacrol and thymol, potent antimicrobial and antioxidant compounds.
research.reference: Arumugam G, Manjula S, Paari K. Biomed Pharmacother. 2016;84:341–349. DOI: 10.1016/j.biopha.2016.09.006. PMC6274163

research.title: Plectranthus amboinicus: A Systematic Review of Traditional Uses, Phytochemical Properties, and Therapeutic Applications
research.summary: Systematic review confirming significant antimicrobial activity of P. amboinicus extracts and essential oils against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, notable antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, and wound healing properties. Validates diverse therapeutic potential across infectious diseases, oncology, and wound care.
research.reference: Filipe MS, Bangay G, Brauning FZ et al. Pharmaceuticals (MDPI). 2025;18(5):707. DOI: 10.3390/ph18050707

research.title: Evaluation of the Effect of Plectranthus amboinicus L. Leaf Extracts on the Bacterial Antioxidant System and Cell Membrane Integrity of Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA01
research.summary: Study demonstrated that P. amboinicus leaf extracts disrupt the bacterial antioxidant system and compromise cell membrane integrity of P. aeruginosa, confirming its potent antimicrobial mechanism of action.
research.reference: Sawant S, Baldwin TC, Metryka O, Rahman A. Pathogens. 2023;12(6):853. DOI: 10.3390/pathogens12060853

comparisonTraits.leaf: Thick, succulent, oval-shaped leaves with scalloped edges; covered in fine hairs; strongly aromatic
comparisonTraits.flower: Small pale blue-purple flowers in loose spikes
comparisonTraits.stem: Fleshy, square cross-section (characteristic of Lamiaceae), green to purplish
comparisonTraits.smell: Strong, pungent oregano-like aroma when leaves are crushed (due to carvacrol and thymol)

name: Mango
shortDescription: A widely cultivated tropical fruit tree whose leaves, bark, and fruit contain mangiferin and other bioactive compounds with scientifically documented antidiabetic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiviral, and cardioprotective properties. Mango leaf extracts have been studied extensively for their health-promoting effects.

preparation.description: Boil 5–10 fresh or dried mango leaves in 2 cups of water for 15 minutes. Strain and drink warm, 1–2 times daily.
Crush fresh bark into a paste and apply to the affected area.
Eat ripe mango fruit fresh for nutritional benefits. Rich in vitamins A, C, and fiber.

facts.origin: South Asia (India, Myanmar, Bangladesh); widely cultivated in tropical regions
facts.habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions; thrives in warm, humid climates

warnings: Mango sap and peel can cause contact dermatitis (allergic skin reaction) in sensitive individuals.
People with latex allergy may also be allergic to mango.
Mango leaves are not a substitute for prescribed diabetes medication.
Consult a doctor before using mango leaf decoction for medicinal purposes.
Pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before use.

cultivationGuide.soil: Deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 5.5–7.5)
cultivationGuide.watering: Regular watering for young trees; mature trees are drought-tolerant
cultivationGuide.growthTime: 3–6 years from grafting; 8–10 years from seed to bear fruit
tips: Protect young trees from frost.
Prune to shape the canopy and improve air circulation.
Apply balanced fertilizer before flowering and after fruit harvest.
Bag fruits on the tree to protect from pests.

research.title: Mangifera indica (Mango)
research.summary: Comprehensive review (cited 690 times) documenting mango's antidiabetic, antioxidant, anti-viral, cardiotonic, hypotensive, and anti-inflammatory properties. Mangiferin, a polyphenolic antioxidant and glucosyl xanthone, is identified as a key bioactive compound responsible for many of these effects.
research.reference: Shah KA, Patel MB, Patel RJ, Parmar PK. Pharmacogn Rev. 2010;4(8):112–118. DOI: 10.4103/0973-7847.70910. PMC3249901

research.title: Multifaceted Health Benefits of Mangifera indica L. (Mango): The Fruit That Should Be Included in Everyone's Diet
research.summary: Review (cited 302 times) providing an overview of the antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer properties of mango. Confirms that mango extracts reduce oxidative stress, inflammation, and cancer cell proliferation through mangiferin and other polyphenols.
research.reference: Lauricella M, Emanuele S, Di Sano C et al. Nutrients. 2017;9(5):525. DOI: 10.3390/nu9050525

research.title: A Review on Ethnopharmacological Applications, Pharmacological Activities, and Phytochemical Composition of Mangifera indica
research.summary: Review (cited 318 times) documenting the ethnopharmacological applications and pharmacological activities of M. indica, including antidiabetic, antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer activities. Identifies mangiferin, quercetin, gallic acid, and phenolic acids as key bioactive constituents.
research.reference: Ediriweera MK, Tennekoon KH, Samarakoon SR. Evid Based Complement Alternat Med. 2017. DOI: 10.1155/2017/6949805

comparisonTraits.leaf: Long, lanceolate, dark green, glossy leaves with prominent midrib; 15–45 cm long
comparisonTraits.flower: Small, pale yellow-pink flowers in large panicles (up to 60 cm long)
comparisonTraits.stem: Tall, evergreen tree up to 30–40 meters with dense canopy; thick, rough, dark gray bark
comparisonTraits.smell: Sweet, fruity aroma from flowers and ripe fruit; leaves have a mild resinous scent

name: Guyabano
shortDescription: A tropical fruit tree whose leaves, seeds, and fruit contain annonaceous acetogenins — powerful compounds with scientifically documented anticancer properties. Extensive research has confirmed cytotoxic activity against various cancer cell lines, along with anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and antidiabetic effects.

preparation.description: Boil 5–10 dried or fresh guyabano leaves in 2 cups of water for 15 minutes. Strain and drink warm, 1 cup 2–3 times daily.
Blend ripe guyabano fruit flesh and drink as juice. Rich in vitamin C, fiber, and natural sugars.
Crush fresh leaves into a paste and apply to the affected area.

facts.origin: Central America, Caribbean, and northern South America; cultivated worldwide in tropics
facts.habitat: Tropical lowlands; thrives in warm, humid environments at sea level to 1,500 m elevation

warnings: Consult a doctor before using for medicinal purposes, especially for cancer.
Guyabano leaf tea is not a substitute for professional cancer treatment.
Excessive consumption of seeds may be neurotoxic (linked to atypical Parkinsonism in some studies).
Avoid use during pregnancy; may cause uterine contractions.
Do not exceed recommended doses; consult healthcare professional for long-term use.
Not a substitute for chemotherapy or prescribed cancer treatment.

cultivationGuide.soil: Deep, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil with good organic matter
cultivationGuide.sunlight: Full sun (6–8 hours daily); tolerates partial shade when young
cultivationGuide.watering: Regular watering; prefers consistent moisture but not waterlogged
cultivationGuide.growthTime: 3–5 years from seed to bear fruit; 2–3 years from grafted tree
tips: Protect from strong winds.
Mulch around the base to retain moisture.
Hand-pollinate flowers for better fruit set.
Harvest fruit when spines begin to separate and color changes to yellowish-green.

research.title: A Review on Annona muricata and Its Anticancer Activity
research.summary: Comprehensive review (cited 124 times) focusing on A. muricata extract's role against various types of cancer, modulation of cellular proliferation and necrosis, and bioactive compounds responsible for anticancer effects. Confirms that acetogenins selectively target cancer cells while sparing normal cells, making it a promising complementary cancer therapy.
research.reference: Ilango S, Sahoo DK, Paital B, Kathirvel K, Gabriel JI. Cancers (MDPI). 2022;14(18):4539. DOI: 10.3390/cancers14184539. PMC9497149

research.title: Anticancer Properties of Graviola (Annona muricata): A Comprehensive Scientific Review
research.summary: Review (cited 262 times) summarizing the current understanding of anticancer effects of A. muricata and its constituents on diverse cancer types. Acetogenins inhibit mitochondrial complex I, selectively targeting ATP-deficient cancer cells. Activity confirmed against breast, prostate, lung, colon, pancreatic, and leukemia cell lines.
research.reference: Radi I, Nair JJ, Che CT, Abbasi AH, Chowdhury S, Akhtar MS. J Exp Pharmacol. 2018;10:115–127. DOI: 10.2147/JEP.S169645. PMC6091294

research.title: Potential Benefits of Annona muricata in Combating Cancer: A Review
research.summary: Review (cited 127 times) exploring A. muricata as a potential complementary cancer treatment agent. Documents anticancer mechanisms including induction of apoptosis, inhibition of angiogenesis, and suppression of tumor growth. Confirms bioactivity across multiple cancer cell lines with acetogenins as the primary active compounds.
research.reference: Yajid AI, Ibrahim TH, Ahmad S, Zainal Abidin Z. Biomed Pharmacother. 2018;104:376–387. DOI: 10.1016/j.biopha.2018.05.074. PMC5862046

comparisonTraits.leaf: Large, oblong, glossy dark green leaves with prominent midrib; 7–20 cm long
comparisonTraits.flower: Solitary, creamy yellow-green, bell-shaped flowers with a strong fruity scent; 3–5 cm long
comparisonTraits.stem: Medium-sized tree up to 6–8 meters; dark gray bark with irregular scaly plates
comparisonTraits.smell: Flowers have a strong, sweet, fruity aroma; leaves have a mild herbal scent when crushed

name: Pansit-pansitan
shortDescription: A succulent annual weed commonly found in gardens and shady areas in the Philippines. Scientifically validated for anti-hyperuricemic (anti-gout), anti-inflammatory, and analgesic properties. University of the Philippines researchers have developed an anti-gout tablet from this plant, which is pending FDA certification.

preparation.description: Boil 1 handful of fresh whole plant in 2 cups of water for 10 minutes. Strain and drink warm, 1 cup 2–3 times daily.
Eat fresh leaves and stems raw as a salad vegetable.
Crush fresh leaves into a paste and apply directly to the affected area.

facts.origin: Tropical Americas; naturalized in tropical regions worldwide
facts.habitat: Shady, moist areas in gardens, lawns, and waste places in tropical regions

warnings: Consult a doctor before using for medicinal purposes.
Not a substitute for prescribed gout medication (e.g., allopurinol, colchicine).
Do not consume in excessive amounts.
Pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before use.
Ensure correct plant identification — some look-alikes may not have the same properties.

cultivationGuide.soil: Moist, rich, well-drained soil; thrives in shaded, humid conditions
cultivationGuide.sunlight: Partial shade to full shade (prefers filtered light)
cultivationGuide.watering: Keep soil consistently moist; does not tolerate drought well
tips: Grows readily in shady garden spots or between stepping stones.
Requires consistent moisture and protection from direct sun.
Harvest the whole plant when flowering for maximum potency.

research.title: Anti-inflammatory and analgesic activity of Peperomia pellucida (L.) Kunth (Piperaceae)
research.summary: Study confirmed significant anti-inflammatory (paw edema induced by carrageenin and arachidonic acid) and analgesic activity (abdominal writhes and formalin tests) of P. pellucida. Effects were dose-dependent and comparable to standard anti-inflammatory drugs. (Cited 167 times)
research.reference: de Fátima Arrigoni-Blank M, Andrade FA, Bolognese AM, Blank AF, Niculau ES, de Aquino AM. J Ethnopharmacol. 2004;91(2-3):215–218. DOI: 10.1016/j.jep.2003.12.010. PMID: 15120441

research.title: Anti-hyperuricemic and Anti-inflammatory Effects of Micropropagated Plants of Peperomia pellucida (L.) Kunth
research.summary: Study demonstrated anti-hyperuricemic activity of P. pellucida leaf extract and anti-inflammatory activity of root extract, indicating its potential as a complementary therapy for gout. (Cited 47 times)
research.reference: Rahmi EP, Rachmawati S, Rahayuningsih E, Widyasari A. Scientia Pharmaceutica. 2020;88(1):9. DOI: 10.3390/scipharm88010009. PMC7092620

research.title: The chemistry and biological activities of Peperomia pellucida (L.) Kunth (Piperaceae)
research.summary: Comprehensive review (cited 98 times) documenting the chemistry and biological activities of P. pellucida, including anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antihyperuricemic, antioxidant, antimicrobial, and antihyperglycemic properties. Key compounds include pellucidin A, a sterol derivative with potent anti-inflammatory activity.
research.reference: Alves NSF, Pereira MCR, da Costa Silva D et al. J Ethnopharmacol. 2019;236:391–408. DOI: 10.1016/j.jep.2019.02.029

comparisonTraits.leaf: Small, heart-shaped, translucent green leaves on thin, watery stems
comparisonTraits.flower: Tiny, spike-like greenish flowers (characteristic of Piperaceae); no petals
comparisonTraits.stem: Translucent, succulent, watery stems that appear almost glass-like
comparisonTraits.smell: Mild, slightly peppery scent when crushed (family Piperaceae)

name: Malunggay
shortDescription: A highly nutritious tree whose leaves are rich in vitamins, minerals, protein, and powerful antioxidants. Scientifically documented to have antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic, antimicrobial, hepatoprotective, and cardioprotective properties. Often called the 'miracle tree' for its exceptional nutritional and medicinal profile.

preparation.description: Add fresh malunggay leaves to soups (tinola, sinigang) during the last 2–3 minutes of cooking to preserve nutrients.
Boil 1 cup of fresh or dried leaves in 2 cups of water for 10 minutes. Strain and drink warm.
Dry leaves in shade, grind into powder. Mix 1 teaspoon into food, drinks, or smoothies daily.

facts.origin: Northern India (Himalayan foothills); cultivated throughout the tropics
facts.habitat: Tropical and subtropical regions; extremely drought-tolerant

warnings: Root bark extract can be toxic in large doses — do not consume roots or bark extracts.
Pregnant women should avoid consuming root bark (may cause uterine contractions).
Consult a doctor before using for medicinal purposes.
Do not replace prescribed medications with malunggay alone.
Pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before use.

cultivationGuide.soil: Well-drained, sandy or loamy soil; tolerates poor and alkaline soil
cultivationGuide.propagation: Seeds, stem cuttings (20–30 cm cuttings root easily)
cultivationGuide.growthTime: Fast-growing; harvestable in 6–8 months from cuttings; produces pods in 6–8 months
tips: Cut back the trunk to 1 meter to encourage bushy leaf growth for leaf harvest.
Prune regularly for continuous leaf production.
Extremely resilient — survives drought, poor soil, and neglect.
Harvest leaves every 2–3 weeks for continuous supply.

research.title: Moringa oleifera: An Updated Comprehensive Review of Its Nutritional and Medicinal Properties
research.summary: Comprehensive review (cited 575 times) documenting M. oleifera's nutritional composition and medicinal properties including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic, antimicrobial, hepatoprotective, cardioprotective, and neuroprotective activities. Confirms it as one of the cheapest and most reliable alternatives for good nutrition.
research.reference: Pareek A, Suthar M, Rathore GS, Bansal V. Nutrients. 2023;15(4):860. DOI: 10.3390/nu15040860. PMC9916933

research.title: Moringa oleifera: A review on nutritive importance and its medicinal application
research.summary: Highly cited review (cited 2,323 times) documenting that M. oleifera provides 7 times more vitamin C than oranges, 10 times more vitamin A than carrots, 2 times more protein than milk, and 4 times more calcium than milk. Confirms antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor properties.
research.reference: Gopalakrishnan L, Doriya K, Kumar DS. Food Sci Hum Wellness. 2016;5(2):49–56. DOI: 10.1016/j.fshw.2016.04.001

research.title: Moringa oleifera is a Prominent Source of Nutrients with Potential Health Benefits
research.summary: Review (cited 506 times) confirming M. oleifera as a rich source of macro- and micronutrients and bioactive compounds including flavonoids, phenolic acids, glucosinolates, and thiocarbamates. Documents antidiabetic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and hepatoprotective properties.
research.reference: Islam Z, Fatima R, Saeed B et al. Int J Food Sci. 2021;2021:6696925. DOI: 10.1155/2021/6696925. PMC8373516

comparisonTraits.leaf: Compound leaves with small, oval leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stem; soft, green, fern-like appearance
comparisonTraits.flower: White, fragrant flowers with yellow centers in loose drooping clusters; about 2.5 cm wide
comparisonTraits.stem: Slender, fast-growing trunk with soft, light gray bark; young stems are green and flexible
comparisonTraits.smell: Mild, slightly horseradish-like scent when leaves or roots are crushed (milder than true horseradish)

name: Bayabas
shortDescription: A tropical fruit tree whose leaves are widely used in Philippine folk medicine as a wash, rinse, or decoction. Laboratory and review evidence supports antimicrobial and gastrointestinal-related activity, but leaf preparations should not replace diagnosis or treatment for persistent diarrhea or infection.

preparation.description: Wash several mature leaves, simmer in water, cool, and use externally as a wash. Traditional use includes wound cleansing; use clean water and seek care for deep or infected wounds.
uses: Traditional wound care and skin cleansing

preparation.description: A mild tea is traditionally prepared from washed leaves. Exact dose and duration should be confirmed with a healthcare professional, especially for children, pregnancy, or concurrent medicines.
uses: Traditional use for diarrhea and stomach discomfort

preparation.description: Cool the strained decoction and use as a rinse; do not swallow large amounts. Dental pain, swelling, fever, or bleeding requires dental or medical evaluation.

facts.origin: Tropical America; now widely cultivated in the Philippines and other tropical regions
facts.habitat: Warm tropical areas, gardens, farms, roadsides, and well-drained soils

warnings: Evidence differs by preparation and is often laboratory or traditional-use evidence.
Do not use as a substitute for oral rehydration or medical evaluation for severe/persistent diarrhea.
Stop if rash, swelling, breathing difficulty, or other allergic symptoms occur.
Pregnant or breastfeeding people, young children, and people taking medicines should consult a clinician before internal use.

cultivationGuide.soil: Well-drained loam or sandy loam; tolerates a range of soils
cultivationGuide.watering: Regular watering while establishing; avoid prolonged waterlogging
cultivationGuide.growthTime: Often fruits in about 2–4 years depending on cultivar and propagation
tips: Prune for airflow and harvest healthy mature leaves away from roads, pesticides, and animal waste.

research.title: Psidium guajava: A Single Plant for Multiple Health Problems of Rural Indian Population
research.summary: This peer-reviewed review summarizes ethnomedical, laboratory, and clinical literature. It reports evidence for guava, especially leaves, in gastrointestinal and infectious conditions, while also reviewing safety data.
research.reference: Daswani PG, Gholkar MS, Birdi TJ. Pharmacognosy Reviews. 2017;11(22):167–174. DOI: 10.4103/phrev.phrev_17_17; PMID 28989253. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5628524/

research.title: Psidium guajava L.: From byproduct and use in traditional medicine to health-promoting applications
research.summary: A review of traditional uses and modern research, including leaf infusions and extracts used for gastrointestinal complaints, wounds, and antimicrobial investigation.
research.reference: Gutierrez-Montiel D et al. Frontiers in Nutrition. 2023;10:1108306. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9902774/

comparisonTraits.leaf: Opposite, oval to elliptical, leathery leaves with prominent veins and a rough upper surface
comparisonTraits.flower: White flowers with many conspicuous stamens
comparisonTraits.stem: Small tree with smooth bark that may peel in patches
comparisonTraits.smell: Aromatic, green, slightly resinous when crushed

name: Kamaria
shortDescription: An aromatic perennial herb known in the Philippines as kamaria or damong maria. Its leaves are used traditionally in washes, poultices, and decoctions; evidence includes phytochemical and preclinical research, while clinical evidence for many traditional claims remains limited.

details.localName: Kamaria / Damong Maria / Maria / Santa Maria

preparation.description: Crush clean leaves or prepare a cooled decoction for external use on minor skin irritation. Do not apply to deep, infected, or heavily bleeding wounds.
Traditional sources describe decoctions, but internal dosing is not standardized. Do not self-dose concentrated preparations.
uses: Traditional use for cough, abdominal discomfort, and dyspepsia

preparation.description: Dried leaves may be used as an aromatic herb; avoid smoke inhalation and do not use moxibustion or concentrated products without trained professional guidance.

facts.origin: Europe, North Africa, and Asia; widely cultivated or naturalized in the Philippines
facts.habitat: Open areas, gardens, roadsides, and disturbed ground in temperate to tropical uplands

warnings: Do not use during pregnancy; traditional sources specifically caution against it because of possible uterine effects.
People allergic to ragweed-family plants may react.
Avoid concentrated essential oil or internal use without professional advice.
Evidence for traditional uses is not equivalent to proof of clinical effectiveness.

cultivationGuide.climate: Tropical highland to temperate; prefers moderate conditions
cultivationGuide.watering: Moderate; allow the surface to dry slightly between watering
cultivationGuide.growthTime: Perennial herb; usable leaves develop within one growing season
tips: Harvest healthy leaves before flowering, avoid contaminated sites, and prune to prevent excessive spread.

research.title: A new sesquiterpene from Artemisia vulgaris
research.summary: The study isolated and characterized a sesquiterpene from A. vulgaris, contributing to the phytochemical evidence base for the plant.
research.reference: Ragasa CY et al. Journal of Natural Medicines. 2008;62:434–436. DOI: 10.1007/s11418-008-0253-0

research.title: Estrogenic Flavonoids from Artemisia vulgaris L.
research.summary: Researchers isolated flavonoids and evaluated estrogen-receptor transcription activity in a laboratory model. This is mechanistic evidence, not proof that leaf preparations safely treat human conditions.
research.reference: Lee SJ et al. Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry. 1998;46(8):3325–3329. DOI: 10.1021/jf9801264

comparisonTraits.flower: Small pale flower heads in branched clusters

name: Lagundi
shortDescription: A Philippine medicinal shrub whose leaves are used in standardized herbal cough products and traditional preparations. Philippine research and DOST-PCHRD documentation describe development and clinical testing of lagundi formulations for cough and respiratory symptoms.

preparation.description: Traditional preparation uses washed leaves simmered in water. Use only appropriately identified plant material, and do not rely on home decoctions for breathing difficulty or persistent fever.
Use only products registered or authorized by the Philippine FDA and follow the product label. Standardized formulations differ from an improvised home decoction.
Crushed leaves or cooled decoction have traditional topical uses; avoid open or infected wounds.
uses: Traditional skin, pain, and inflammation care

facts.origin: South and Southeast Asia, including the Philippines
facts.habitat: Tropical and subtropical scrub, riverbanks, roadsides, and home gardens

warnings: Seek urgent care for shortness of breath, blue lips, chest pain, severe wheezing, or high/persistent fever.
Use standardized products only as directed; do not assume a home decoction has the same dose or evidence.
Consult a clinician if pregnant, breastfeeding, treating a child, or taking multiple medicines.
Stop if allergic symptoms or worsening respiratory symptoms occur.

cultivationGuide.growthTime: Shrub establishes within one to two years; flowering depends on climate
tips: Prune after flowering, maintain airflow, and harvest mature leaves from pesticide-free plants.

research.title: Lagundi: Anti-cough and anti-asthma medicine
research.summary: The Philippine Council for Health Research and Development reports that UP/NIRPROMP researchers developed lagundi formulations and conducted scientific studies and clinical trials for cough and asthma-related symptoms.
research.reference: Philippine Council for Health Research and Development, DOST. HeaRTNovation technology profile. https://www.pchrd.dost.gov.ph/heartnovation/lagundi-anti-cough-and-anti-asthma-medicine/

research.title: A systematic review on Vitex negundo (NIRPROMP formulations) for acute cough of mild to moderate severity in pediatric patients
research.summary: The systematic-review literature evaluates NIRPROMP lagundi formulations in pediatric acute cough. Findings should be interpreted according to formulation, dose, study quality, and clinician guidance.
research.reference: Systematic review record and evidence synthesis; verify the final published citation before academic submission. https://www.herdin.ph/index.php?option=com_herdin&view=publiclistowp&layout=list&type=researches&searchstr=lagundi+for+cough

comparisonTraits.leaf: Usually palmately compound, commonly with five lance-shaped leaflets and a gray-green underside
comparisonTraits.flower: Small bluish-purple flowers in terminal clusters
comparisonTraits.stem: Woody, branched shrub with gray-brown bark
comparisonTraits.smell: Aromatic, slightly camphoraceous when crushed

name: Madre Cacao
shortDescription: A fast-growing leguminous tree used in Philippine traditional medicine, particularly as a leaf juice, decoction, or topical preparation for skin conditions such as scabies. Recent Philippine evidence synthesis found that G. sepium was probably comparable to 5% sulfur in complete lesion clearance, but herbal treatment must not replace proper scabies diagnosis and contact treatment.

preparation.description: Traditional use applies expressed leaf juice externally. Do not apply to eyes, mucous membranes, extensive broken skin, or infants without professional guidance.
Prepare a cooled wash from clean leaves for external use only. Wash clothing and bedding and seek medical care for suspected scabies because household contacts may need treatment.
uses: Traditional management of itchy skin conditions

preparation.description: Pounded leaves may be used as a short-term topical poultice in traditional practice; discontinue if burning, rash, or swelling occurs.
uses: Traditional topical antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory use

facts.origin: Tropical America; widely planted and naturalized in the Philippines
facts.habitat: Tropical lowlands, farms, hedgerows, roadsides, and agroforestry systems

warnings: Do not ingest leaves or concentrated preparations; use is primarily topical in Philippine traditional practice.
Scabies requires correct diagnosis, treatment of close contacts, and laundering of clothes/bedding.
Patch-test topical preparations and stop if irritation occurs.
Do not use on children, pregnancy, or extensive skin disease without clinician advice.

cultivationGuide.soil: Well-drained soil; tolerates relatively poor soils
cultivationGuide.growthTime: Fast-growing tree; may reach usable size within one to two years
tips: Plant away from utility lines, prune regularly, and avoid harvesting from chemically treated trees.

research.title: Efficacy and Safety of Gliricidia sepium, Senna alata, and Tinospora rumphii in the Treatment of Filipino Patients with Scabies: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
research.summary: This 2025 systematic review included Filipino randomized trials. For G. sepium, pooled data suggested probably no difference in complete clearance compared with 5% sulfur, with no serious adverse events reported across included studies.
research.reference: Pasion GCS, Montilla LP, Genuino RF. Acta Medica Philippina. 2025;59(18):16–37. DOI: 10.47895/amp.vi0.11461; PMID 41502969. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12772372/

research.title: Phytochemical analysis of three common medicinal plants including Gliricidia sepium
research.summary: The study analyzed phytochemicals in selected Philippine medicinal plants, including G. sepium, contributing preliminary chemical evidence but not clinical proof of effectiveness.
research.reference: Raju R et al. Scholars Academic Journal of Biosciences. 2021;9(3):84–88. https://academia.edu/download/81025842/SAJB_93_84-88.pdf

comparisonTraits.flower: Pink to lilac pea-like flowers, often appearing before new leaves
comparisonTraits.stem: Woody tree with gray-brown bark and branching crown

name: Sambong
shortDescription: An aromatic Philippine shrub whose leaves are traditionally prepared as a decoction and used in cough, fever, urinary, and kidney-stone-related remedies. DOST-PCHRD and peer-reviewed studies describe diuretic and anti-lithogenic research, but suspected kidney stones require medical evaluation.

preparation.description: Wash leaves and prepare a mild decoction; use only as directed by a qualified professional or authorized product label.
uses: Traditional cough, fever, and urinary support

preparation.description: Use only a properly labeled and authorized preparation, following dosage instructions. Do not combine with diuretics without medical advice.
uses: Traditional diuretic and kidney-stone prevention support

preparation.description: Aromatic leaves may be used traditionally for congestion, but avoid smoke or steam burns and do not delay care for breathing difficulty.

facts.origin: South and Southeast Asia, including the Philippines
facts.habitat: Open sunny areas, grasslands, roadsides, and disturbed tropical ground

warnings: Seek medical care for severe flank pain, fever, vomiting, blood in urine, or difficulty urinating.
Diuretic use can affect hydration and interact with medicines; ask a clinician before use.
Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding, kidney disease, or heart failure without professional guidance.
Evidence for dissolving stones is largely preclinical or formulation-specific; do not claim it cures stones.

cultivationGuide.growthTime: Fast-growing perennial shrub; harvestable leaves develop within months
tips: Harvest mature leaves from clean plants before heavy flowering; dry in shade with good airflow.

research.title: Blumea balsamifera—A Phytochemical and Pharmacological Review
research.summary: This peer-reviewed review summarizes traditional uses, phytochemicals, pharmacology, and safety questions for B. balsamifera, including use in the Philippines as sambong.
research.reference: Pang Y et al. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2014;2014:789843. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6272021/

research.title: Effect of Blumea balsamifera extract on the phase and morphology of calcium oxalate crystals in vitro
research.summary: An in vitro study examined effects of B. balsamifera extract on calcium oxalate crystals, providing laboratory evidence relevant to anti-lithogenic claims but not proof of clinical stone treatment.
research.reference: Montealegre CM, De Leon RL. Asian Journal of Urology. 2017;4(4):201–207. DOI: 10.1016/j.ajur.2016.08.009; PMID 29387552. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5772838/

name: Serpentina
shortDescription: In Philippine herbal-medicine sources, serpentina commonly refers to the intensely bitter herb Andrographis paniculata, especially its leaves and aerial parts. The common name is ambiguous and can also refer to Rauvolfia serpentina, so the scientific name must be checked before use.

preparation.description: Traditional preparations use bitter leaves or aerial parts, but dosing is not standardized for home use. Do not self-treat prolonged fever or suspected infection.
uses: Traditional fever, cold, digestive, and liver-related uses

preparation.description: Use only a properly labeled, authorized product and follow its directions. Confirm that the label identifies Andrographis paniculata, not Rauvolfia serpentina.
uses: Investigational or traditional immune and respiratory support

preparation.description: Topical uses are less established than oral traditional uses; avoid application to broken skin unless advised by a healthcare professional.

facts.origin: South and Southeast Asia, including the Philippines
facts.habitat: Tropical gardens, cultivated plots, open grassland, and disturbed ground

warnings: The name serpentina is ambiguous; misidentification can be dangerous.
Andrographis may cause gastrointestinal upset or allergic reactions and may interact with medicines.
Avoid during pregnancy unless specifically approved by a clinician; use caution with blood-pressure, anticoagulant, immune, or diabetes medicines.
Seek care for high fever, breathing problems, dehydration, jaundice, or worsening symptoms.

cultivationGuide.watering: Regular but moderate; avoid waterlogged soil
cultivationGuide.propagation: Seeds, usually started in nursery beds and transplanted
cultivationGuide.growthTime: Annual or short-lived herb; leaves harvestable after several months
tips: Harvest before or during early flowering, label the plant by scientific name, and avoid roadside or pesticide-contaminated plants.

research.title: Harnessing the medicinal properties of Andrographis paniculata for diseases and beyond: a review of its phytochemistry and pharmacology
research.summary: This review covers traditional use, andrographolide and other constituents, pharmacological studies, and safety considerations. Much evidence is preclinical or formulation-specific.

research.title: Andrographis paniculata (Burm. f.) Wall. ex Nees: A Review of Ethnobotany, Phytochemistry, and Pharmacology
research.summary: A peer-reviewed review summarizes use for common cold, fever, diarrhea, and other conditions and discusses phytochemicals, pharmacology, and toxicity. It does not establish that raw leaves cure disease.
research.reference: Hossain MS et al. The Scientific World Journal. 2014;2014:274905. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4408759/

name: Calamansi
shortDescription: A small citrus fruit tree widely cultivated in the Philippines, contains vitamin C, but evidence that calamansi preparations prevent or treat infection is limited and preparation-specific.

preparation.description: Extract juice from fresh fruits and mix with warm water and honey.
Apply fresh juice directly to the skin.

facts.habitat: Tropical lowlands and agricultural areas

warnings: Highly acidic; may cause gastric irritation if consumed in large amounts on an empty stomach.

tips: Prune regularly to maintain shape and encourage fruit production.

research.title: Phytochemicals, Bioactive Properties and Commercial Utilization of Calamondin
research.summary: Calamansi (Citrus microcarpa) has been investigated mainly through phytochemical, antioxidant, antimicrobial, and essential-oil studies. A recent review describes bioactive compounds in calamondin but does not establish that juice or leaf preparations prevent respiratory infection. A Philippine herbal reference records traditional uses, while clinical dosing and efficacy remain insufficiently established. Evidence therefore supports cautious traditional use, not claims of an immune cure.
research.reference: Venkatachalam K et al. Plants. 2023;12:1751. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10146261/

name: Pandan
shortDescription: A tropical plant with fragrant, blade-like leaves used extensively in Southeast Asian cooking and traditional medicine for relaxation and pain relief.

preparation.description: Boil 3-4 tied leaves in 2 cups of water for 10 minutes. Drink warm.
Steep crushed leaves in warm coconut oil.

facts.habitat: Tropical gardens, near water sources

warnings: Culinary use is common, but medicinal doses and long-term safety are not well established; avoid concentrated preparations during pregnancy or with medicines without professional advice.

cultivationGuide.growthTime: Fast-growing, usable leaves in a few months
tips: Thrives in humid environments; protect from severe drought.

research.title: Antimicrobial potentials of Pandanus amaryllifolius Roxb.
research.summary: Research on Pandanus amaryllifolius is predominantly phytochemical and preclinical. A 2024 review reports antimicrobial activity in extracts and identifies phenolic and other compounds, but the findings do not prove that pandan tea treats anxiety, arthritis, or headaches in people. Culinary use is distinct from standardized medicinal dosing.
research.reference: Wahyuni DK et al. Journal of Applied Pharmaceutical Science. 2024. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11324095/

research.title: Botany, phytochemistry, pharmacology, and applications of Pandanus amaryllifolius

name: Aloe Vera
scientificName: Aloe vera (L.) Burm.f. [synonym: Aloe barbadensis Mill.]
shortDescription: A succulent plant well-known for its clear gel, whose inner gel has been studied for topical skin applications; effectiveness varies by condition and product.

preparation.description: Slice a leaf open and apply the clear inner gel directly to the skin.
Blend the clear inner gel (avoiding the yellow latex) with water.

facts.habitat: Arid and semi-arid regions

warnings: Avoid consuming the yellow latex (aloin) just under the skin, as it is a strong laxative and can cause severe cramping.

cultivationGuide.watering: Low; allow soil to dry completely between watering
tips: Highly susceptible to root rot if overwatered.

research.title: Aloe Vera: Usefulness and Safety
research.summary: Topical aloe gel is generally well tolerated, but clinical results differ by condition and product. The U.S. NCCIH states that oral aloe latex can cause abdominal pain, cramps, and diarrhea; oral leaf extracts have also been linked to cases of acute hepatitis. The yellow latex should not be confused with purified inner-leaf gel, and aloe should not be taken orally during pregnancy without medical advice.
research.reference: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health. NIH. https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/aloe-vera

research.title: Aloe vera: A review of toxicity and adverse clinical effects

name: Tamarind
shortDescription: A large tropical tree whose leaves are traditionally used in decoctions to treat fevers, malaria, and wound infections.

preparation.description: Boil a handful of fresh leaves in water for 15 minutes. Use the liquid as a wash or drink in small amounts.
Pound fresh leaves and apply to wounds or swollen joints.

facts.habitat: Tropical savannas and monsoon forests

warnings: Consult a doctor if fever persists; highly acidic leaves may irritate sensitive skin.

tips: Requires a distinct dry season for best growth and pod production.

research.title: Anti-inflammatory and analgesic potential of Tamarindus indica Linn. (Fabaceae): a narrative review
research.summary: Reviews describe antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and analgesic findings for different Tamarindus indica parts, including leaves, but much of the evidence is laboratory or animal research. Tamarind leaf decoction should not be presented as a treatment for malaria; suspected malaria requires testing and appropriate antimalarial therapy. Topical use on broken or infected wounds also requires caution.
research.reference: Komakech R et al. Integrative Medicine Research. 2019;8:100273. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6704379/

comparisonTraits.flower: Small yellow flowers with red or orange streaks

name: Kamias
shortDescription: A fruit-bearing tree closely related to starfruit, used medicinally for its leaves and highly acidic fruits to manage inflammation and skin conditions.

preparation.description: Crush fresh leaves into a paste and apply topically.
Boil fruits and use the liquid for a warm bath or drink in very small quantities.

facts.habitat: Tropical lowlands

warnings: Fruits are extremely high in oxalates; consuming large amounts can cause acute kidney injury.

tips: Protect young trees from strong winds.

research.title: Acute oxalate nephropathy due to Averrhoa bilimbi fruit juice
research.summary: Averrhoa bilimbi fruit is highly acidic and concentrated juice has been associated with acute oxalate nephropathy and kidney injury in case reports. These reports concern ingestion, not proof that the leaves are medicinally effective. The document should therefore avoid recommending bilimbi juice as a drink, especially for people with kidney disease, dehydration, or medicines affecting renal function.
research.reference: Bakul G et al. Indian Journal of Nephrology. 2013;23(4):302–304. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3741977/

name: Niyog-niyogan
shortDescription: A climbing vine famous in the Philippines as an effective traditional anthelmintic (deworming) agent.

preparation.description: Eat mature, dried seeds two hours after a meal (Adults: 8-10 seeds, Children: 4-5 seeds).
Boil leaves and use as a wash.

facts.habitat: Thickets, secondary forests

warnings: Do not exceed the recommended dose of seeds, as overdose causes severe hiccups, dizziness, and abdominal pain.

tips: Requires a strong trellis or support structure.

research.title: Niyogniyogan (Quisqualis indica L.) as an Anthelminthic
research.summary: Niyog-niyogan seeds have a long history of traditional use against intestinal worms, and reviews describe anthelmintic activity in laboratory and animal models. However, older traditional dose instructions are not equivalent to current clinical guidance, and seed toxicity and misidentification are concerns. Persistent abdominal symptoms or suspected parasitic infection should be assessed and treated using approved medicines.
research.reference: Guerrero LE. Philippine Journal of Science. 1924. https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/full/10.5555/19242901104

name: Banaba
shortDescription: A tropical tree whose leaves contain corosolic acid and have been studied for glucose-related effects; this is not proof that homemade tea treats diabetes.

preparation.description: Boil dried leaves in water for 15 minutes. Drink as a tea up to 3 times a day.
Boil the bark and use the liquid for digestive issues.

facts.habitat: Riverbanks, secondary forests

warnings: Monitor blood sugar closely if taking alongside prescribed diabetes medication to prevent hypoglycemia.

cultivationGuide.soil: Tolerates poor soils, prefers well-drained loam
tips: Makes an excellent ornamental shade tree due to its large floral displays.

research.title: A Review of the Efficacy and Safety of Banaba (Lagerstroemia speciosa L.) and Corosolic Acid
research.summary: Banaba leaf extracts and corosolic acid have been studied for glucose-related effects. A review of clinical and preclinical evidence concluded that results are promising but limited by small studies, varying preparations, and uncertain dosing. Banaba tea must not replace prescribed diabetes therapy; people using glucose-lowering medicines should consult a clinician and monitor for hypoglycemia.
research.reference: Stohs SJ, Miller H, Kaats GR. Phytotherapy Research. 2012;26(3):317–324. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22095937/

name: Tanglad
shortDescription: A fragrant tropical grass used as a culinary herb and traditional medicine for digestive issues, fever, and high blood pressure.

Pound the stalks and leaves, apply to painful areas.

facts.habitat: Tropical savannas and cultivated gardens

warnings: Generally safe; however, essential oil must be diluted before applying to the skin.

tips: Cut stalks at the base rather than pulling the whole root system.

research.title: Ethnopharmacology, phytochemistry, and biological activities of Cymbopogon citratus
research.summary: Lemongrass contains citral and has been investigated for antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and blood-pressure-related effects. A comprehensive review notes that evidence ranges from in vitro and animal work to limited clinical observations, and that safety requires further characterization. Lemongrass tea should not be used to replace antihypertensive treatment; essential oil is much more concentrated than tea and should not be swallowed.

name: Makabuhay
shortDescription: A climbing vine recognized by its notably warty stems, known for its bitter taste and traditional use in several conditions; evidence and safety are limited, and it should not be used to treat malaria without antimalarial care.

preparation.description: Boil a small piece of the stem in water. Drink in very small quantities due to intense bitterness.
Crush the stem and extract the juice, or boil to make a wash. Apply to the skin.

facts.habitat: Primary and secondary tropical forests

warnings: Extremely bitter. Do not consume in large doses; toxic to the liver in excess. Pregnant women should avoid it entirely.

tips: Plant near trees or fences for the vine to climb.

research.title: Tinospora crispa (L.) Hook. f. & Thomson: A Review of Its Ethnobotany, Phytochemistry, and Pharmacology
research.summary: Tinospora crispa has traditional and preclinical pharmacological literature, but liver injury is a major safety concern. A review of reported cases concluded that incorrect identification and use of Tinospora species may cause severe hepatic injury or death. Makabuhay should not be self-administered internally for malaria, ulcers, or fever, and jaundice, dark urine, or severe abdominal pain requires urgent medical care.

name: Gumamela
shortDescription: A widely cultivated ornamental plant in the Philippines, used traditionally for treating boils, mumps, and respiratory issues.

preparation.description: Crush fresh flower petals and leaves into a sticky paste and apply locally.
Boil flowers and leaves in water for 10 minutes.

facts.habitat: Cultivated gardens, tropical environments

warnings: Use only clean, correctly identified, pesticide-free material externally; evidence for internal use is limited and allergic or irritant reactions are possible.

research.title: Evaluation of the wound-healing activity of Hibiscus rosa-sinensis L. in rats
research.summary: A rat wound-healing study found that a Hibiscus rosa-sinensis extract improved wound contraction and epithelialization compared with controls. This is preclinical evidence and does not establish that a homemade poultice treats boils, mumps, bronchitis, or infected wounds. Use clean material only, avoid deep or infected wounds, and seek medical care when systemic symptoms are present.

name: Suha
shortDescription: A large citrus fruit whose fruit, peel, and leaves are used traditionally; evidence for medicinal effects varies, and pomelo may interact with some medicines.

preparation.description: Boil leaves or dried rind in water. Drink warm.
Boil fresh leaves and add the aromatic water to a bath.

facts.habitat: Lowland tropical forests, river valleys

warnings: Like grapefruit, pomelo juice can interact with certain medications (e.g., statins, blood pressure drugs).

tips: Requires heavy fertilization and consistent watering during fruit development.

research.title: Citrus maxima (Burm.) Merr. (Rutaceae): Bioactive Chemical Constituents and Pharmacological Activities
research.summary: A review of Citrus maxima summarizes phytochemicals and pharmacological studies involving fruit, peel, seed, and other parts. Pomelo and grapefruit-related citrus can affect drug metabolism through furanocoumarins; the interaction risk depends on the product and medicine. Do not assume that pomelo leaf or peel decoction is a safe substitute for treatment, and ask a pharmacist about interactions.

name: Alugbati
shortDescription: A leafy green vegetable with a mucilaginous texture, rich in vitamins, and used traditionally for mild digestive issues and burns.

preparation.description: Add leaves to stews and soups as a vegetable.
Mash fresh leaves to extract the mucilage (slime) and apply topically.

facts.habitat: Tropical lowlands

warnings: Safe as a food source; no known significant toxicity.

tips: Provide a trellis; the plant thrives in extreme heat where true spinach bolts.

research.title: Pharmacognostical Standardization of Upodika—Basella alba L.
research.summary: Basella alba is primarily a food plant. Pharmacognostic research has characterized its leaves and stem, and reviews describe nutrient, mucilage, antioxidant, and other preliminary pharmacological findings. These data do not prove that leaf poultices heal burns or that the plant treats anemia. Cooked leaves may be included as food, but burns and persistent constipation require appropriate care.
research.reference: Shantha TR et al. Pharmacognosy Journal. 2016;8(1):1–7. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5255969/

research.title: A review of the taxonomy, ethnobotany, phytochemistry and pharmacology of Basella alba

name: Tuba-tuba
shortDescription: A hardy shrub used in folk medicine primarily for external wound healing, though its seeds are highly toxic.

preparation.description: Warm the leaves over a fire until wilted, rub with a little coconut oil, and apply externally.
Apply the clear/yellowish sap directly to a wound.

facts.habitat: Wastelands, dry tropical regions

warnings: EXTREMELY TOXIC SEEDS: Eating even a few seeds can cause severe vomiting, diarrhea, and death. Sap may irritate sensitive skin. Never take internally without expert supervision.

tips: Often planted as a living fence; requires virtually no maintenance.

research.title: Ethnobotany, ethnopharmacology and toxicity of Jatropha curcas L. (Euphorbiaceae)
research.summary: Jatropha curcas has a documented toxicity literature. Seeds and seed products can cause severe gastrointestinal poisoning, and latex or oil may irritate skin and eyes. Although laboratory studies have examined leaves and topical traditional uses, evidence is not sufficient to recommend sap on open wounds. This plant should be clearly labeled and kept away from children and animals.
research.reference: Abdelgadir HA, Van Staden J. South African Journal of Botany. 2013;88:204–218. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sajb.2013.07.021

name: Katakataka
shortDescription: A unique succulent famous for producing tiny plantlets along its leaf margins, used widely as an anti-inflammatory poultice.

preparation.description: Pound fresh leaves and apply directly to the affected area.
Squeeze juice from lightly roasted leaves and drop onto affected skin.

facts.habitat: Tropical and subtropical gardens, rocky areas

warnings: Generally safe for external use. Internal consumption should be supervised, as excessive intake may cause gastric distress.

cultivationGuide.sunlight: Bright, indirect light to full sun
cultivationGuide.watering: Low; allow soil to dry completely
cultivationGuide.propagation: Leaf cuttings, plantlets falling from leaves
tips: Highly invasive in favorable climates; best kept in pots.

research.title: A Genus of Plants Known as ‘Miracle Leaf’: Kalanchoe
research.summary: Kalanchoe pinnata is also known as Bryophyllum pinnatum. Reviews report traditional anti-inflammatory and wound-related uses, but the evidence base is largely preclinical, and some Kalanchoe species contain bufadienolides that raise toxicity concerns. A topical preparation should be used only on minor intact skin and stopped if irritation occurs; internal use requires professional advice.
research.reference: de Andrade EA et al. Plants. 2023;12:2518. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10383218/

name: Dila-dila
shortDescription: A small ground herb characterized by a rosette of leaves flat against the earth, traditionally used as a diuretic and fever reducer.

preparation.description: Boil the entire cleaned plant (or just roots) in water for 15 minutes. Strain and drink.
Pound fresh leaves and apply topically.

facts.habitat: Open grasslands, pastures, disturbed grounds

warnings: Consult a doctor if symptoms of urinary tract infections persist; ensure correct identification, as it grows among common weeds.

cultivationGuide.soil: Sandy or loamy, tolerates poor soils
tips: Forages easily in lawns and fields; rarely deliberately cultivated.

research.title: Anti-neuroinflammatory Activity of Elephantopus scaber L. via Inhibition of NF-κB and MAPK Signaling
research.summary: Elephantopus scaber research includes anti-inflammatory, neuroinflammatory, antioxidant, and other preclinical studies. An animal toxicology section in one study reported no abnormal clinical signs at tested doses, but that does not establish human safety or efficacy. Dila-dila should not be used to self-treat urinary infection, fever, edema, or ulcers without diagnosis.
research.reference: Chan CK et al. 2017. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5478732/

name: Insulin Plant
shortDescription: A tropical leafy plant used in folk medicine for glucose-related purposes; available evidence is mainly preliminary and it must not replace prescribed diabetes treatment.

preparation.description: Wash 1 fresh leaf thoroughly and chew it well before swallowing. Typically done in the morning and evening for a set period.
Dry the leaves in the shade, grind them into a powder, and boil 1/2 to 1 teaspoon of the powder in a cup of water. Strain and drink.

facts.origin: Eastern Brazil (widely cultivated in India and Southeast Asia)
facts.habitat: Tropical gardens, shaded and humid environments

warnings: NOT a replacement for medical insulin. Do not stop taking prescribed diabetes medications.

Monitor blood sugar levels very closely if consuming this plant while taking antidiabetic drugs, as the combination can cause dangerous hypoglycemia (dangerously low blood sugar). Pregnant or breastfeeding women should avoid use without consulting a doctor.

cultivationGuide.soil: Rich, moist, well-draining soil with high organic matter
cultivationGuide.sunlight: Partial shade to bright indirect light (avoid harsh afternoon sun)
cultivationGuide.watering: High; keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged
cultivationGuide.growthTime: Fast-growing; leaves can be harvested within 2-3 months of planting
tips: Spreads via underground rhizomes. Grow in a shaded area of the garden or in large pots to control its spread.

research.title: Effect of the insulin plant (Costus igneus) leaves on dexamethasone-induced hyperglycemia
research.summary: The “insulin plant” name refers to Costus igneus in older literature; current taxonomy commonly uses Chamaecostus cuspidatus. A small human study and animal studies reported glucose-lowering effects, but the evidence is not sufficient to replace insulin or prescribed diabetes medicines. Any use alongside diabetes treatment requires glucose monitoring and clinician supervision to reduce hypoglycemia risk.
research.reference: Shetty AJ et al. Journal of Clinical and Diagnostic Research. 2010. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2924971/
